newsitem.title: USA: Florida Legislature to focus on school funding.
newsitem.headline: Florida Legislature to focus on school funding.

text.p: Florida's Legislature convenes Tuesday with Republicans in control of both houses for the first time in more than 120 years.
Republican leaders have vowed not to raise taxes, but the state's expanding economy is expected to generate $1 billion of new revenues, putting the budget total at $42 billion for fiscal 1998.
School construction funding is expected to dominate the agenda during the 60-day session. A state survey identified $3.3 billion of building needs over the next five years.
Florida public school enrollment has soared from 1.5 million in 1980 to 2.2 million today and is projected to hit 2.5 million by 2010.

Several funding proposals were already announced. An education commission appointed by Democrat Gov. Lawton Chiles proposed expanding the gross receipts tax on utilities to cover water, sewage, garbage collection and cable TV service.
The 2.5 percent tax currently applies only to telephone, electric and gas service and raises $600 million a year to back Florida Board of Education Bonds for school contruction.
Expanding the tax, which would be phased in over five years, would raise $179 million a year, enough to issue $1.3 billion of new bonds.

House Appropriations Chairman Rudy Garcia, R-Hialeah, has proposed raising the property tax local governments can collect for school construction. Since 1980, school boards have been allowed to collect $2 per $1,000 of assessed value. Garcia's proposal would increase that to $2.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, raising an additional $250 million statewide.
Senate Democrat Leader Ken Jenne of Fort Lauderdale is drafting legislation to give school boards $1 of lottery proceeds for every $1 of local taxes dedicated to school construction.
Sen. Howard Forman, D-Pembroke Pines, is promoting a plan to let school boards levy additional taxes on real estate transaction by raising documentary stamp tax.
House Speaker Dan Webster, R-Orlando, has proposed cutting costs elsewhere by $50 million and allocating that money for shcool construction.
--raising the tax on cigarettes by 10 cents a pack, to 43.9 cents a pack, to fund an anti-smoking campaign targeting children.
--cutting the tax eployers pay to fund Florida's unemployment compensation program, which has a $1.9 billion surplus or enough to pay benefits for three years.
--cutting or eliminating the intangibles tax on stocks and bonds, which is $2 per $1,000 of market value.

--increasing state funding by $30 million for the high-speed rail system that would link Miami, Orlando and Tampa. The state has already pledged $70 million to the system, which could not be built unless Congress agrees to back the bonds.
